commonsFile: File:006 Dune 45 in Sossusvlei at sunrise Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg
alt: Red star dune lit by sunrise light with the Namib dune sea behind
caption: Dune 45 at sunrise, 45 km beyond the Sesriem gate. It is the easiest of the great Namib dunes to climb before the heat arrives, and the opening morning of the desert section of this route.

alt: Dead camel thorn trees on a white clay pan under red dunes with a moon in the sky
caption: Deadvlei: camel thorn trees dead for several centuries stand on a white clay pan walled by dunes. It is reached on foot from the 4x4-only end of the Sossusvlei road, and in February-March a rare rain can leave the pan briefly wet.

alt: Narrow sandstone and conglomerate canyon cut by the Tsauchab river
caption: Sesriem Canyon, a gorge cut by the Tsauchab river a few kilometres from the NWR campsite. It makes a shaded, cool walk for the hottest part of a Sesriem afternoon.

commonsFile: File:Flamingos and pelicans in Walvis Bay 03.jpg
alt: Flamingos and pelicans feeding in shallow water at Walvis Bay
caption: Flamingos and pelicans in the Walvis Bay lagoon, a Ramsar-listed wetland just before Swakopmund. The cool, foggy coast is a deliberate contrast to the inland desert heat.

alt: Aerial view of dunes meeting the Atlantic lagoon at Sandwich Harbour
caption: Sandwich Harbour from the air: the Namib dunes plunge directly into the Atlantic. The tide-dependent dune and beach driving is done with a local guided 4x4 operator rather than in the group's own vehicle.

alt: Dense colony of Cape fur seals on rocks and beach at Cape Cross
caption: The Cape Cross Cape fur seal colony on the Skeleton Coast road north of Henties Bay. It is a loud, smelly, close-range stop that sets the cold-coast mood before turning inland.

alt: Natural rock arch framing granite peaks at Spitzkoppe
caption: The granite inselbergs and rock arch of Spitzkoppe. The community-run campsite lets the group sleep among the boulders, with rock-painting sites reachable on foot with local guides.

alt: Ancient animal engravings on a sandstone rock face
caption: Rock engravings at the UNESCO-listed Twyfelfontein site, one of the largest concentrations of rock art in Africa. Visits are with a local guide, which is the main way the site's community earns income.

alt: Desert-adapted elephant spraying sand over itself in a dry riverbed
caption: Desert-adapted elephants range along the dry rivers of the Kunene Region. In Feb-March they are widely dispersed, so sightings from Twyfelfontein are possible but not guaranteed.

commonsFile: File:Zebras and springboks at the Okaukuejo Waterhole, Etosha National Park, Namibia.jpg
alt: Zebras and springbok drinking at the floodlit Okaukuejo waterhole
caption: Zebra and springbok at Okaukuejo's famous waterhole. In the green season animals spread across the park, so permanent waterholes like this are the reliable places to sit and watch.

commonsFile: File:Elephant family at Gemsbokvlakte waterhole, Etosha National Park, Namibia.jpg
alt: Elephant family at a waterhole in Etosha
caption: An elephant family at a waterhole in Etosha. Self-driving between waterholes from the Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni camps is the core of the park days.

alt: Wide desert landscape and gravel road near Solitaire
caption: The gravel roads around Solitaire, the fuel stop between Windhoek and Sesriem. This is the kind of C- and D-road driving that dominates the trip and that the 80 km/h advice applies to.
